source.title: M3Former: Fine-Grained Cross-Layer Mixing for Transformers
source.authors: Jia-Song Han; Yun-Kai Chai; Tong Zhu; Hengyu Zhang; Wei Fang; Jin-Tao Wang; Guo-Qi Li; Yu Cheng

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. There are minor PDF-extraction and table-formatting artifacts, but they do not prevent reading the results.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures held-out loss across model sizes and training-token budgets, and compares architectures at fixed sizes. Its results also challenge the claim that architecture details change loss only slightly: cross-layer connection changes produce substantial loss differences.
record.gate_note: The study reports validation-loss scaling measurements and fits a power law to five Transformer sizes. The size sweep couples parameter count with training tokens at 20 tokens per parameter, and the token sweep spans 5N–20N. Downstream evaluations are reported, but the paper does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss. The averaging interventions in §5.4 are not rows for the claim versions because they do not measure power-law scaling or fixed-parameter architecture differences.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper, but it fits L(N)=E+A(N/1e8)^−α to five pre-norm Transformers (81M–1.36B non-embedding parameters) at 20 tokens per parameter on FineWeb-Edu and reports the fit quality (RMSE 0.002). That is a result on V1 in a new setting (WSD schedule, FineWeb-Edu). The fit mainly serves as a tool for 'equivalent size'. No other version is tested. The cross-layer connection comparisons change the connection mechanism, not shape (depth, width, heads at fixed N), so they do not measure V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that M3Former lowers held-out loss at every dense size from 100M to 1.4B, matching a Transformer 1.19–1.34x its size. They find it beats MUDDFormer, including at 1.4B with PrePostNorm, and attention residuals, and that it carries over to MoE models up to 4.6B. They conclude that all three broadcast constraints matter, with the first group split capturing most of the per-parameter gain. Downstream averages improve modestly; larger scales, longer training and other modalities are left as limitations.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture study, not a replication of either original scaling-law study. It trains pre-norm decoder-only models on a fixed FineWeb-Edu sample, generally at 20 tokens per parameter, and compares residual-connection variants.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model size, connection method, token budget, and normalization: MUDDFormer diverges at 1.4B with the shared pre-norm recipe but completes with PrePostNorm; the M3 group-count choice also varies across sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing the residual connection with token-dependent cross-layer mixing lowers loss at 20N by 0.031–0.085 (M3, +1.4–3.9% parameters), 0.028–0.080 (MUDDFormer) and 0.0005–0.047 (attention residuals). The paper expresses this as matching a Transformer 1.19–1.34x larger. MUDDFormer diverges at 1.4B under pre-norm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Changes to the residual/cross-layer connection mechanism shift the loss-versus-size curve by an effective-size multiplier, at little parameter cost.

record.problems: The dense sweep reaches 1.4B and spans less than two orders of magnitude in parameters; parameter count and training-token budget are coupled in the main size comparison. Token budgets span only 5N–20N. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the main scaling-loss results and uses one fixed FineWeb-Edu sample.
record.rows_left_out: No reported validation-loss rows were omitted. Downstream task scores in Tables 3 and 8 are not extracted because the paper does not test their predictability from scale or pretraining loss. The coefficient-averaging interventions in §5.4 and Figures 6 and 11 do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: Parameters, tokens and compute are not varied independently (N is tied to D=20N). The size range is about 1.2 decades, not several orders. No token-scaling or compute fit is made. The 5N–20N sweep spans only 4x.
No small-run fit is checked against much larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation search; 20N is taken from Hoffmann et al.
Depth, width and head shape are not varied at fixed N. Cross-layer connection variants are a different construct.
English text pretraining only. The MoE models are not fitted for scaling.
Downstream scores are reported at two dense sizes and two MoE sizes, but there is no relation to scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents across setups.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'challenges' label is removed. The comparisons change the connection mechanism and add parameters; they are not shape variations at fixed N. Even so, the gains are about 1–3% of loss, arguably 'slight'. Token-sweep rows are recoded from 'partial' to 'cannot_determine': loss falls monotonically, but no power law is fitted, and the 5N/10N runs are decay branches of the 20N run. No uncertainty is reported for the losses.

versions.untested_parts: The parameter sweep uses a fixed 20-token-per-parameter ratio, so parameters are not varied independently of tokens and compute. The token sweep covers 5N–20N rather than several orders of magnitude. The paper does not fit power laws to the token sweep or test compute scaling independently.
No small-run fit is evaluated against the observed loss of a substantially larger run.
The paper does not search for a loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or fit allocation trends.
The comparisons change cross-layer connection and residual-read structure, not a broad range of depth and width choices or other architecture details.
The study uses decoder-only language models pretrained on English text; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but no relationship or predictive fit between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss is tested.
The study does not vary fitting choices or compare fitted exponents across setups, nor test whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.note: The fitted curve uses five sizes and a fixed 20N-token-per-parameter training ratio.

relationships.condition: Five dense pre-norm Transformers, 81M–1.36B non-embedding parameters, 20 tokens per parameter, FineWeb-Edu, WSD schedule
relationships.reason: A saturating power law (α=0.164, E=0.965) fits the five held-out losses with RMSE 0.002 (r01). Evidence is weak: 3 parameters, 5 points, about 1.2 decades.
relationships.display_finding: A three-parameter saturating power law with exponent 0.164 and floor 0.965 fits five held-out losses with RMSE 0.002 across about 1.2 decades.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Five standard Transformer sizes trained at 20 tokens per parameter
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a power-law fit to held-out loss with RMSE 0.002 across the tested sizes (r01).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Token-budget sweep at fixed model sizes and size sweep at a fixed token-per-parameter ratio
reader_labels.reason: Loss falls as tokens increase from 5N to 20N, but this is not a several-orders-of-magnitude sweep or a fitted token law; the parameter sweep also couples parameters and tokens (r02–r16, r17–r31).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Fixed-size comparisons of Transformer, M3Former, attention residuals, and MUDDFormer at 20N
reader_labels.reason: Changing the cross-layer/residual architecture yields reported loss differences of up to 0.085 versus the Transformer, and MUDDFormer also diverges at 1.4B under the shared recipe (r19, r22, r25, r28, r31–r41).
